opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I think for a long time physics has been extraordinarily successful with a reductionist program: you break things down into their smallest constituents, you find the fundamental laws governing those pieces, and you assume that, in principle, everything else follows. And that worked beautifully for particle physics, for a lot of condensed matter, for things where you can write down a clean Hamiltonian and solve it, or at least approximate it well.

But the interesting frontier now, at least to me, is that "in principle" part. Knowing the microscopic rules doesn't actually give you a tractable handle on what emerges at larger scales. Life, intelligence, economies, even a lot of non-equilibrium physics: these are systems that are driven, open, dissipating energy, constantly far from equilibrium. And the textbook equilibrium statistical mechanics we inherited doesn't really describe them well.

So I see the complex systems view as asking a different question. Instead of "what are the fundamental particles," it's "what are the general principles by which matter self-organizes when you pump energy through it?" There's this beautiful line of work in non-equilibrium thermodynamics, things like Jeremy England's ideas around dissipative adaptation, fluctuation theorems, that suggests systems that are better at capturing and dissipating free energy tend to be statistically favored. That's almost a thermodynamic account of why complexity, and eventually life and intelligence, arise at all.

And coming from quantum computing and physics-based AI, I think that lens is also practically important. If you view computation itself as a physical process, then learning, inference, generative modeling are all things that matter does when it's driven out of equilibrium. Rather than fighting the noise and the thermodynamics, you can harness them. So for me the complex systems approach isn't a departure from physics; it's physics growing up to address the systems we actually care about, the ones that are messy, adaptive, and alive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses computation as a physical process, but does not present the universe as a quantum computer running a program or self-simulation.

r002.rationale: It says microscopic rules do not provide a tractable handle on emergent behavior, but does not state that predicting it can require computation comparable to the physical system itself.

r003.rationale: The response describes complex systems as messy and difficult to handle, but does not say that computational models can be as opaque as the systems they model.

r004.rationale: It does not describe using a programmable parametric complex system to model a natural system.

r005.rationale: The response advocates a complex-systems perspective and harnessing physical processes for computation, but does not propose shifting physicists’ roles from finding a unifying theory to building computers or software.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we've spent the better part of a century trying to understand the universe by taking it apart. Reductionism has been incredibly successful, right? We went down to quarks, to the Standard Model, and it works beautifully. But at some point you hit a wall where going smaller doesn't give you more explanatory power. The interesting phenomena, the things we actually care about, like life, intelligence, turbulence, even gravity in some of the emergent pictures, those don't live at the bottom of the stack. They live in the organization, in how the parts interact and what structure arises from that.

So my view is that the next frontier for physics isn't a smaller particle, it's understanding emergence itself. How do you get stable, complex, information-processing structures out of simple local rules? Thermodynamics was actually the first complex systems theory if you think about it. Boltzmann didn't track every molecule, he asked what the statistics of the whole thing look like, and out of that came entropy, free energy, the arrow of time. I think there's a similar move waiting to be made at a much larger scale, where you treat the universe as a computation and ask what it's optimizing for, how information flows, where the attractors are.

And the reason I'm optimistic about it now, rather than it just being a nice philosophical stance, is that we finally have the tools. Machine learning is essentially a laboratory for emergence. You take simple units, you couple them, you add a gradient, and you get behavior nobody programmed in. That's a physics experiment. Neural networks, thermodynamic computing, these are all ways of actually simulating and probing complex systems rather than just writing equations we can't solve. So I see it less as abandoning physics and more as physics getting its hands on the right instruments for the hard part of the problem.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that knowing the microscopic laws isn’t the same as understanding what a system will actually do. You can know the interactions between individual particles and still have a very hard time explaining how collective behavior emerges—how you get a fluid, a living organism, or something that processes information.

A complex systems approach puts those questions at the center. How do different scales interact? Which details matter at a particular scale, and which can you forget? How do stable structures arise in systems that are continually exchanging energy with their environment?

That doesn’t mean abandoning fundamental physics. It means connecting the underlying laws to the organization we actually observe. Statistical mechanics already gives us a powerful example of that: you move from microscopic interactions to macroscopic descriptions with entirely new, useful concepts.

So, to me, the opportunity is to extend that way of thinking to systems that are far from equilibrium, that adapt, and that have feedback. We want to understand not just what the constituents are, but how their interactions produce new forms of collective behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think physics has been incredibly successful at breaking things down into their constituent parts and finding simple laws for those parts. But knowing the microscopic laws doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens when you put a huge number of interacting components together. You get collective behavior, emergent structure, and effective descriptions that become useful at different scales.

Life is a particularly striking example. An organism obeys the laws of physics, but that alone doesn’t explain how it maintains itself, processes information, or adapts. You have to think about an open system exchanging energy and matter with its environment, operating far from equilibrium.

So, for me, the complex systems approach is about connecting those levels of description. How do microscopic dynamics give rise to macroscopic organization? When can we compress all that complexity into a few meaningful variables? Statistical mechanics already gives us a powerful example of how to do that. The opportunity is to extend that kind of thinking to systems that evolve, learn, and organize themselves.
